summary: Defines an SMIv2 Management Information Base module for Reliable Server Pooling. The framework has two protocols, ASAP and ENRP, and this MIB lets administrators monitor them. It is an Experimental document.

plainLanguage.summary: A group of backup servers should stay healthy. This note defines the gauges used to check on them, so administrators can see how the pool is doing.

subtitle: Monitoring tools for reliable server pools using SNMP.

tldr.problem: Reliable Server Pooling frameworks need a way for administrators to monitor the health and status of ENRP servers, pool elements, and pool users via standard management protocols.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 5525 defines an SMIv2-compliant Management Information Base module with tables and objects that expose the state of RSerPool implementations through SNMP.
tldr.outcome: Network administrators can use standard SNMP tools to monitor pool health, server uptime, element load, and registration status without specialized RSerPool tools.

today: RFC 5525 is an Experimental document, as is the broader RSerPool framework it monitors. The MIB specification remains the standard way to instrument RSerPool implementations for SNMP-based monitoring.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
Reliable Server Pooling (RSerPool) is a framework that helps distribute client requests among a pool of servers, with automatic failover if a server fails. The RSerPool framework consists of two protocols: ASAP (Aggregate Server Access Protocol) for client-to-pool communication, and ENRP (Endpoint Handlespace Redundancy Protocol) for pool management.

RFC 5525 defines a Management Information Base (MIB) module that allows network administrators to monitor RSerPool implementations using the Simple Network Management Protocol (SNMP). The MIB provides access to managed objects running on ENRP servers, pool elements, and pool users, enabling visibility into the health and status of the RSerPool infrastructure.
sections.plainLanguage: Think of the MIB as a dashboard showing how your backup server system is working. It tells administrators when servers are up, how busy they are, and how long they've been running.

sections.title: MIB Structure
sections.content:
The RSerPool MIB is organized into three main branches, each monitoring a different component of the RSerPool infrastructure:

rserpoolENRPServers provides information about ENRP server instances, including their operation scope, identifier, port numbers, and registered pools. For each pool, the MIB tracks pool elements (servers) and their addresses for both ASAP and ENRP communication. It also tracks peer ENRP servers and their connectivity status.

rserpoolPoolElements contains information about pool element instances running on a host, including the pool handle, element identifier, transport ports, policy settings, load information, and addresses used for service communication.

rserpoolPoolUsers monitors instances of applications that access pools, tracking their operation scope, target pool handle, and uptime.

This three-branch structure allows administrators to monitor different types of RSerPool components depending on which hosts are running which services.
sections.plainLanguage: The MIB has three sections: one for pool managers, one for server nodes, and one for clients. Each section shows different information about what's happening with that part of the system.

sections.title: Key Managed Objects
sections.content:
The MIB defines numerous managed objects for monitoring RSerPool state. Critical objects include:

Server status objects monitor ENRP server uptime, port numbers for ASAP and ENRP announcements, and which addresses each server uses for advertising. Pool element objects track element identifiers, registration lifetime (how long the element remains registered), home ENRP server assignment, transport protocol and port information, and policy-related metrics like weight and load.

The MIB also provides address tables that list the IP addresses (both IPv4 and IPv6) associated with each ASAP transport endpoint, ENRP endpoint, and user service endpoint. These tables enable administrators to see all addresses through which a component is reachable.

Policy objects expose the pool selection policy identifier, description, weight (for weighted selection policies), current load, and load degradation values, allowing administrators to verify how traffic distribution is configured.
sections.plainLanguage: The MIB tracks things like: Is the server running? How busy is it? What's its internet address? What rules decide which server gets the next request?

sections.title: Operational Use
sections.content:
The RSerPool MIB is an Experimental track module because the RSerPool framework itself is experimental. Administrators who deploy RSerPool implementations can use SNMP agents that expose this MIB to monitor their infrastructure in real time.

The MIB includes both read-only objects (for monitoring) and read-write objects. Read-write objects such as pool handle, description, policy identifier, policy weight, and registration lifetime can be configured via SNMP SET operations, allowing some management of the pool through standard tools. However, these objects should be maintained persistently if the implementation supports it; that is, changes should survive a reboot.

Administrators should configure SNMP access control appropriately, since modifications to pool configuration can have operational impact.
sections.plainLanguage: Administrators can use SNMP tools to watch their RSerPool system and even make changes to how it's configured, as long as they have permission.

sections.title: Security Implications
sections.content:
Several MIB objects can alter RSerPool behavior if modified. Changing a pool element's pool handle, policy identifier, weight, load degradation, or registration lifetime can disrupt load balancing or pool membership. Modifying textual descriptions through SNMP could mislead administrators about system state.

All readable objects in the MIB expose information about the RSerPool infrastructure, and unauthorized SNMP reads could reveal network topology and pool composition. The RFC recommends using SNMPv3 with full cryptographic protection for both authentication and privacy when managing RSerPool implementations. SNMPv1 and SNMPv2c lack adequate security mechanisms.

Implementations should restrict SNMP access to the MIB to authorized management systems only, using SNMPv3 authentication and encryption rather than community-string-based access control.
sections.plainLanguage: Anyone who can read the SNMP data learns about your server setup. Anyone who can change it could break your pool. Use strong encryption and authentication to protect it.
